arbitrate.e: From Latin arbitratus, past participle of arbitrari (“to be a witness, act as umpire”), from arbiter (“umpire”); see arbiter.
arbitrate.g: To make a judgment (on a dispute) as an arbitrator or arbiter

arch.e: From Middle English arch, arche, from Old French arche (“an arch”), a feminine form of arc, from Latin arcus (“a bow, arc, arch”).
From the prefix arch-. "Principal" is the original sense; "mischievous" is via onetime frequent collocation with rogue, knave, etc.

archangel.e: From Middle English archangel, from Old French archangele, from Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos) from Ancient Greek prefix ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”). By surface analysis, arch- + angel.
archangel.g: A powerful angel that leads many other angels, but is still loyal to a deity, and often seen as belonging to a particular archangelical rank

archer.e: from Middle English archer, archere, from Old French archier, from Vulgar Latin *arcārius, alteration of arcuārius, from Latin arcus (“bow”).
archer.g: One who shoots an arrow from a bow or a bolt from a crossbow.

architect.e: From Middle French architecte, from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”). By surface analysis, archi- + -tect.
architect.g: A professional who designs buildings or other structures, or who prepares plans and superintends construction.

area.g: A measure of the extent of a surface; it is measured in square units.

aren't.e: Spelling replacement of the homonym an’t.
aren't.g: A contraction of “am not”, used e.g. in the construction "aren’t I?"

argue.e: From Middle English arguen, from Old French arguer, from Latin arguere (“to declare, show, prove, make clear, reprove, accuse”), q.v. for more.
argue.g: To show grounds for concluding (that); to indicate, imply.

argument.e: From Middle English argument, from Anglo-Norman and Old French arguement, from Latin argumentum. The English word is analysable as argue + -ment.
argument.g: A fact or statement used to support a proposition; a reason.

argument.e: The obsolete senses are derived from Middle English argumenten (“to argue, discuss; to consider, reflect”), from Old French argumenter (“to argue”), from Latin argūmentārī (“to adduce arguments or proof, prove, reason; to adduce (something) as argument or proof; to conclude”), from argūmentum (“argument (for a position); evidence, proof; point, theme.
argument.g: To put forward as an argument; to argue.

argumentative.e: From Late Middle English argumentatif (“syllogistic, sophistic”), from Old French argumentatif, argumentative (modern French argumentatif (“argumentative”)) and Medieval Latin, Late Latin argūmentātīvus, from Latin argūmentātor + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives).
argumentative.g: Of or relating to argumentation; specifically, presenting a logical argument or line of reasoning; argumentive, discursive.

arid.e: From French aride or directly from Latin āridus (“dry, arid, parched”), compare its synonymous contracted form ardus. Originally from the verb āreo (“to be dry, to be parched”), akin to ārdeō (“to be on fire, to burn”).

aright.e: From Middle English ariȝt, ariht, from Old English āriht (“aright, properly”), from earlier *an riht, on riht (“rightly”), corresponding to a- + right.
aright.g: Rightly, correctly; in the right way or form.

aright.e: From Middle English arighten, arihten (“to raise up”); and Middle English iriȝten, irihten, ȝerihten (“to make right, correct, erect”), from Old English ġerihtan (“to set right”), equivalent to a- + right.
aright.g: To make right; put right; arrange or treat properly.

arise.e: From Middle English arisen, from Old English ārīsan (“to arise, get up; rise; spring from, originate; spring up, ascend”), from Proto-Germanic *uzrīsaną (“to rise up, arise”), equivalent to a- + rise. Eclipsed Middle English sourden, sorden, borrowed from Old French sordre, sourdre (“to arise, originate, fly up”).
arise.g: To come up from a lower to a higher position.

ark.e: From Middle English arke, from Old English earc, ærc, from Latin arca (“chest, box, coffer”), from arceō (“to enclose”).
ark.g: A large box with a flat lid.

arm.e: From Middle English arm, from Old English earm (Anglian arm), from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz (“arm”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“a fitting, joint; arm, forequarter”), a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to join, fit together”).
arm.g: The portion of the upper human appendage, from the shoulder to the wrist and sometimes including the hand.

arm.e: Back-formation from arms (plural), from Middle English armes, from Old French armes, from Latin arma (“weapons”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo-, a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to fit together”), hence ultimately cognate with etymology 1.

armed.e: From arm (“to equip with a weapon”) + -ed.

armhole.e: From Middle English arme hole, armehole, arm hole, arm-hole, armhole, arm-hool(e), armole, harmehole; equivalent to arm + hole.

armlet.g: A band worn on the arm for ornamental or identification purposes.

armor.e: From Middle English armure, armour, armor, armeure, borrowed from Anglo-Norman armure and Old French armeüre, from Latin armātūra. By surface analysis, arm (“to cover or furnish”) + -or (suffix forming agent nouns or nouns of quality, state, or condition).
armor.g: A protective layer over a body, vehicle, or other object intended to deflect or diffuse damaging forces.

armourbearer.g: One who carries armor for another.

armoury.e: From Middle English armerie, armurie, armorye, from Anglo-Norman armurrie, from armure (“arms, armor”) + -ie (“-y”). By surface analysis, armour + -y.
armoury.g: A place where arms are kept, an arsenal.

armrest.g: Part of the seat of a chair that is designed to support the arm.

arms.e: From Middle English armes, from Old French armes, from Latin arma (“weapons”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo-, a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to fit together”), hence ultimately cognate with etymology 2.

army.e: From (1386) Middle English armee, borrowed from Old French armee (cf. modern French armée), from Medieval Latin armāta (“armed force”), a noun taken from the past participle of Latin armāre (“to arm”), itself related to arma (“tools, arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join, fit together”).
army.g: A large, highly organized military force, concerned mainly with ground (rather than air or naval) operations.

aroma.e: From Late Latin arōmata (“spices”) (or arōma (“spice”)), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).
aroma.g: A smell; especially a pleasant, spicy or fragrant one.

around.e: From Middle English around, arounde, from a- (from Old English a- (“on, at”)) + Middle English round (“circle, round”) borrowed from French, equivalent to a- + round.
around.g: Forming a circle or closed curve containing (something).

arrange.e: From Middle English arengen, arrangen (“to draw up a battle line”), borrowed from Old French arengier, arangier (“to put in a line, put in a row”), derived from reng, rang, ranc (“line, row, rank”), from Frankish *hring (“ring”).
arrange.g: To set up; to organize; to put into an orderly sequence or arrangement.

array.e: From Middle English arrayen, from Anglo-Norman arraier (compare Old French arraier, areer (“to put in order”)), from Vulgar Latin *arrēdō (“to put in order, arrange, array”), from *rēdum (“preparation, order”), from Frankish *raid or *raidā (“preparation, order”) or Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌸𐍃 (garaiþs, “ready, prepared”), from Proto-Germanic *raidaz, *raidiz (“ready”).

arrest.e: From Middle English arest (noun) and aresten (verb), from Old French areste (noun) and arester (“to stay, stop”, verb), from Vulgar Latin *arrestō, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (“back”) + stō (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”), equivalent to ad- + rest.
arrest.g: A check; a stop; an act or instance of arresting something.

arrival.e: From Middle English arivaile, arivaille, arrival, arryvaile, arryvaylle, aryvayle, aryvaylle, from Middle French arrivaille, from arriver. By surface analysis, arrive + -al.
arrival.g: The act of arriving (reaching a certain place).

arrive.e: From Middle English arriven, ariven, from Old French ariver, from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre (“to land, come ashore”), derived from Latin rīpa (“shore, river-bank”). For the semantic evolution, compare Old English ġelandian, ġelendan, lendan (“to arrive at land; land”) > Middle English alenden, landen (“to arrive; arrive at shore; land”).
arrive.g: To reach; to get to a certain place.

arrogance.e: From Middle English arrogaunce, from Middle French arrogance, from Latin arrogantia.
arrogance.g: The state of being arrogant; a type of extreme or foolish pride in which someone feels much superior to another.

arrogant.e: From Middle English arrogaunt, from Old French arrogant, from Latin arrogāns, present active participle of arrogō.
arrogant.g: Having excessive pride in oneself, often with contempt or disrespect for others.

arrow.e: From Middle English arwe, from Old English earh (“arrow”) (oblique form ēarw-), from Proto-West Germanic *arhu (“arrow”), from Proto-Germanic *arhwō (“arrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érkʷo- (“bow, arrow”).
arrow.g: A projectile consisting of a shaft, a point and a tail with stabilizing fins that is shot from a bow.
Contraction of ever + a, sometimes used with a redundant a or an.

art.e: From Middle English art, from Old English eart, second-person singular present indicative of wesan. Further etymology uncertain, see are.

article.e: From Middle English article, from Old French article, from Latin articulus (“a joint, limb, member, part, division, the article in grammar, a point of time”), from Latin artus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂értus (“that which is fit together; juncture, ordering”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join, fit (together)”).
article.g: A piece of nonfiction writing such as a story, report, opinion piece, or entry in a newspaper, magazine, journal, encyclopedia, etc.

articulate.e: Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

artificer.e: From Middle English artificer, from Middle French artificier, from Latin artificiarius.
artificer.g: Someone who is skilled in their trade; an artisan.

artificial.e: From Middle English artificial (“man-made”), borrowed from Old French, borrowed from Latin artificiālis, from artificium (“art; skill; talent”) + -ālis.
artificial.g: Man-made; made by humans; of artifice.

artillery.e: From Middle English artillerie, from Old French artillerie (“collection of military engines, crossbows, lances etc.”), from artillier (“to equip, provide with contraptions”), alteration of atiller (“to arrange, adjust, put on clothes or, especially, pieces of armour”) (influenced by art), itself from Vulgar Latin *apticlō < **apticulō.
artillery.g: Large projectile weapons, in modern usage usually large guns, but also rocket artillery.

artistic.e: Borrowed from French artistique, from artiste + -ique. By surface analysis, artist + -ic.
